O.outcome_detail: educational attainment, including years of schooling and college completion

result.effect: PGS-outcome correlation approximately 0.4; about 15% of individual differences explained; college completion 60% in the top PGS decile versus 10% in the bottom decile

cells.quote: More importantly, a “polygenic score ” (PGS) derived from the estimated effects of the DNA variants in the study explains about 15% of individual differences in out-of-sample prediction, among people who are genetically of European descent. This means that the correlation between outcome (the number of years of schooling or attaining college completion) and the PGS is approximately 0.4, using only a DNA sample as information. Indeed, the difference in prevalence of college completion between individuals in the top decile versus bottom decile of the distribution of the PGS was 50% (60% versus 10%) 3, which is huge.
cells.note: The study reports an association, not a manipulated treatment effect.

O.outcome_detail: shared family environmental influence on secondary school attainment and equality of opportunity

cells.quote: Their main result, using state-of-the-art statistical modelling, was that the effect of shared family environment was substantially reduced among twins whose tracking was delayed until a later age. The results are consistent with the hypothesis that delayed streaming improves equality of opportunity by reducing the effect of prior family environmental influence.
cells.note: The author states that the conclusion is indirect and that the design did not permit a direct estimate of the causal effect of delayed tracking.

O.outcome_detail: learning trajectory across 100 days of cognitive practice

cells.quote: The main novelty of this study is in the design because it was too small to draw any meaningful conclusions from the empirical data presented, as recognised by the authors. A sample size of the order of thousands might be required to quantify genetic effects on baseline performance and subsequent learning.
cells.note: The study included adults aged 20–80 and repeated assessments over 100 days; the text does not report a dependable directional result.
